question: Which statement best describes How specificity is calculated?
options: When multiple rules set the same property on an element, the cascade picks a winner in order: importance (including !important), then specificity, then source order. The cascade is what makes a large stylesheet deterministic — there's always a defined winner, never a coin flip.

Specificity is a score with columns: inline styles, then ids, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then type/element selectors and pseudo-elements. Read it like a tuple (a, b, c, d): count ids, then classes, then types. A higher value in an earlier column always wins, regardless of lower columns.

To compare two selectors, compare their columns left to right. One id (0,1,0,0) beats any number of classes (0,0,10,0) because the id column is higher. This is why a single #id rule can stubbornly override dozens of class rules — and why id-based styling causes pain.

When two rules have equal specificity and importance, the one that appears later in the source (or is linked later) wins. This is why stylesheet order matters and why override styles are placed after base styles. It's the final tiebreaker in the cascade.

Some properties (color, font-family, line-height) are inherited by descendants automatically; others (margin, padding, border) are not. Inheritance is separate from specificity — an inherited value loses to ANY directly matching rule on the element. The keywords inherit, initial, and unset let you control inheritance explicitly.

question: Which statement best describes Source order?
options: A 'specificity war' happens when escalating selectors (ids, !important, deep chains) fight to override each other, making CSS unmaintainable. The cure is to keep specificity low and flat: prefer single classes, avoid ids and !important for styling, and rely on source order for intentional overrides.
